What is the quad-core economy?

It is a way of describing four technologies as layers of one system: artificial intelligence plans, robotics acts, satellite networks connect, and Bitcoin settles. The term comes from strategy writing, not from a standard. This report uses it as a frame and checks each layer against cited sources.
How do AI agents work?

An AI agent is a language model placed in a loop. It reasons about a goal, calls a tool such as a search engine or an API, reads the result, and repeats until the goal is met. Retrieval supplies facts the model was not trained on, while permissions, evaluation and human approval keep its actions within limits.
How do warehouse robots avoid colliding?

A fleet manager plans every robot’s route together. Multi-agent path-finding algorithms such as conflict-based search plan each robot’s path, detect where two robots would occupy the same cell at the same time, and replan with a constraint that makes one of them wait or go around.
How much does it cost to launch a kilogram into orbit?

According to a NASA analysis, the Space Shuttle cost about $54,500 per kilogram to low Earth orbit, a Falcon 9 lists at about $2,720 per kilogram and a Falcon Heavy at about $1,400. Those figures assume a full payload, so small satellites pay more per kilogram.
How does low-Earth-orbit satellite internet work?

Thousands of satellites orbit a few hundred kilometres up, close enough for low delay. A user terminal steers a beam to a passing satellite, which forwards the data by laser to neighbouring satellites and down to a ground station near the destination. Routes are recalculated continuously because the satellites are always moving.
How does Bitcoin proof-of-work work?

Miners assemble transactions into a block and repeatedly hash the block header with a different nonce until the result falls below a target set by the network. Finding such a hash takes an enormous number of attempts, but checking it takes one. The target adjusts every 2,016 blocks to keep blocks about ten minutes apart.
Can AI agents make payments on their own?

Technically, yes. The L402 protocol lets a web service request a small Lightning payment and lets a program pay and continue without a card or an account. It is an emerging approach, not common practice, and any production system should cap what an agent can spend and require human approval above that cap.
Does Algorythmos build robots, satellites or Bitcoin infrastructure?

No. Algorythmos designs and operates the AI layer: agents, data pipelines, evaluation and MLOps. This report is an independent analysis of public sources and is general information, not financial or investment advice.

AI as the Control Plane for Physical Systems
How to engineer an AI agent that directs robot fleets, satellite telemetry and payments: tool contracts, durable state, limits and evaluation.
11 October 2026
The agent is the easy part

Our evidence report on AI, robotics, space and Bitcoin describes four technologies as layers of one system, with AI as the control plane. The figures behind it are public: 78% of organisations reported using AI in 2024, and 5 million industrial robots were in operation at the end of 2025. What those figures do not show is the engineering between the layers.

A language model in a loop can plan a delivery in seconds. Making that plan safe to execute, when a tool call can start a robot or release a payment, is where the work is. Four design decisions carry most of it.
1. Tools with contracts
An agent acts only through tools, so each tool is a contract: typed inputs, typed outputs, and a clear statement of what it changes in the world.
Separate read tools from write tools. Reading fleet status is free; dispatching a robot is not.
Make write tools idempotent, so a retried call cannot dispatch the same pick twice.
Return structured errors the model can reason about, not free text.
2. State that survives a dropped link
Physical work outlasts a model’s context window and any single network connection. Satellite links extend coverage, but they do not remove delay or outages.
Keep the job’s state in a durable store, not in the conversation.
Treat telemetry as events with timestamps, and decide explicitly what to do when they arrive late or out of order.
Define a safe default for silence: a robot that hears nothing stops.
3. Limits on money and motion
Protocols such as L402 make it technically possible for a program to pay for a service. That is a reason for limits, not for trust.
Give each agent a spending cap per job and per day, enforced outside the model.
Require a person to approve any step above a threshold, and record who approved it.
Log every tool call with its inputs, outputs and cost, so the run can be audited afterwards.
4. Evaluation before autonomy
An agent earns autonomy the way a model earns production: by passing tests that someone wrote down in advance.
Replay recorded jobs and compare the agent’s plan with what a competent operator did.
Inject failures on purpose: a blocked aisle, a lost link, a rejected payment.
Track the same metrics in production, and roll back when they move.
Where to start

Start with one workflow and read-only tools. Let the agent propose plans that a person executes, and measure how often the proposals are accepted unchanged. Add write tools one at a time, each behind an approval step, once that number is high enough to justify it.
The full analysis, with the sources for every figure and five step-through diagrams of the underlying algorithms, is in the evidence report.

How Signals Travel: Fibre, Satellites & AI
Evidence report: how sound, fibre, radio and satellite lasers carry data, and whether data centres in orbit could replace fibre. 17 sources.
Evidence report · Infrastructure analysis
Infrastructure
Global
Signal physics, networks and where AI compute sits

Every answer an AI system gives is a signal that has to travel: from a voice to a microphone, through glass under an ocean, sometimes up to a satellite and across to another by laser. Headlines about laser-linked constellations and data centres in orbit suggest that fibre is about to be replaced. Most of them skip the physics, mix deployed systems with prototypes, and repeat company figures as if they were measurements. Anyone deciding where a model should run, or which link it can depend on, needs to know which parts are established and which are still an experiment.

This report follows one message through each physical carrier and explains the mechanism at every step: sound as a pressure wave [5], the loudspeaker that reverses it [6], light and radio as one spectrum [3, 4], fibre under the sea [1, 7], radio and laser links in orbit [8, 10, 11], and the first prototype of computing in space [15, 16, 17]. Each popular claim is then set against its source and given one of five verdicts: established physics, deployed, demonstrated, company-reported, or thought experiment. The conclusion is a layered network, not a replacement: submarine cables carry over 99% of international data flows [13], and satellites add reach and resilience on top.

How an engagement would run: we work on the software and data layer only. Algorythmos does not build cables, satellites or ground stations; we build the models, pipelines and monitoring that run on top of them. Discovery maps one decision, the telemetry behind it and what a person must still approve.
Link and fleet health. Telemetry from links, terminals or satellites feeds anomaly and drift detection, so a degrading link is flagged before it drops traffic.
Traffic and capacity forecasting. Demand, weather and outage history feed forecasts for routes that mix fibre, radio and satellite, with stated error bars.
Placement of compute. For each model we work out where it should run (device, gateway, data centre or on board) from the bandwidth, latency and cost of the link under it.
Paperwork and operations. Document intelligence for licensing, spectrum and landing-permit files, and agent workflows for operations runbooks, each with an audit log and human approval.

A message is a pattern, not a substance. Air molecules oscillate about fixed positions while the sound moves outward [5], and a loudspeaker rebuilds that pattern with a coil, a magnet and a diaphragm [6]. No receiver needs the original molecules, electrons or photons.

Radio, microwaves, light and X-rays are the same radiation at different wavelengths [3, 4], and it behaves as a wave in some experiments and as photons in others [2]. A microwave oven uses it to deliver energy, not a message [9].

Fibre is the backbone and will stay so on current evidence: submarine cables carry over 99% of international data flows [13], and the ITU is working on making them more resilient, not on replacing them [14].

Satellite links are real and mixed. Starlink uses radio to reach customers and publishes up to 200 Gbps for each laser link between satellites [8]. NASA sent video by laser from 19 million miles away at 267 Mbps and completed that experiment in September 2025 [10]. Clouds still interrupt laser links to the ground [11].

Computing in orbit is one prototype. Google launched a single test satellite on 1 October 2026 to measure how its AI chips cope with radiation and temperature [17], and plans two more in 2027 [16]. That is evidence of a serious experiment, not of an orbital data centre.

1. Sound: a pattern in the air

Speech begins as a change in air pressure. Sound in air is a longitudinal wave: the molecules oscillate about their equilibrium positions while the disturbance moves outward [5]. A microphone turns that pressure into a changing voltage. An analogue-to-digital converter measures the voltage at regular intervals and stores the measurements as numbers, a codec compresses them, and software cuts the result into packets. At the far end a loudspeaker runs the process backwards: the signal current flows through a voice coil that sits in a magnet’s field and is fixed to a diaphragm, so the coil and diaphragm move and push the air [6]. What arrives is the pattern, rebuilt, not the air that left the speaker’s mouth.
Sampling and quantisation: measure the voltage many thousands of times a second and round each reading to a number.
Compression codecs: keep what the ear needs and discard the rest, so speech fits in a small data stream.
Packetisation: split the stream into addressed, time-stamped pieces that a network can route and reorder.

Microphones, converters and loudspeakers are mature parts made at very large scale. The competition is now in software: codecs, noise suppression and speech models small enough to run on the device itself.

Sound fades quickly with distance, echoes, and offers little bandwidth. It can carry data, as dial-up and underwater acoustic modems show, but slowly. Every stage adds some noise or distortion, so the far end hears a reconstruction that is close enough to understand, not a perfect copy.
2. Waves, fields and photons: one spectrum

Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are all electromagnetic radiation; they differ in wavelength [3]. Along the spectrum, frequency and energy rise as wavelength falls: NASA’s reference chart puts radio below about 3 × 10⁹ Hz and gamma rays above about 3 × 10¹⁹ Hz [4]. The same radiation acts as a wave under some conditions and as a beam of photons under others, and both descriptions are needed [2]. To carry data, a transmitter changes a property of the wave on purpose (its amplitude, phase, frequency or polarisation) and the receiver measures the result and estimates which symbols were sent. A microwave oven uses the same radiation for a different purpose: a magnetron produces microwaves, water molecules in the food vibrate, and that produces heat. It does not make food radioactive [9].
Modulation: encode bits as controlled changes in amplitude, phase, frequency or polarisation.
Multiplexing: send many channels at once on different frequencies or wavelengths through one medium.
Error-correcting codes: add structured redundancy so the receiver can detect and repair damaged bits.

The everyday pictures mislead. A photon is not a bead with part of the message written on it, and the receiver does not need the same photons that left the transmitter. Losing some of them lowers the signal against the noise; the engineering question is whether enough signal remains to tell the symbols apart.
3. Fibre: light guided through glass

Glass fibres had been used since the 1930s, but lost too much light to carry information far. In the 1960s Charles Kao showed that fibres of very pure glass would carry enough of it, work that earned him half of the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physics [1]. The other ingredient arrived on 16 May 1960, when Theodore Maiman built the first working laser [12]. In a modern link a transmitter modulates a laser and the fibre guides the light, which weakens and spreads as it goes. Long routes are built as a chain of spans. Optical amplifiers raise the power of the light without decoding it, and add some noise as they do; regenerators, where used, detect the data, decide each symbol again and send a fresh signal. The ITU publishes design guidelines for submarine systems of this kind [7]. The result is the backbone of the internet: submarine cables carry over 99% of international data flows [13].
Wavelength-division multiplexing: many colours of light share one fibre, each carrying its own channel.
Coherent detection: read the phase and polarisation of the light as well as its brightness, to carry more bits per symbol.
Forward error correction: the receiver repairs errors without asking for the data again.

Routes and landing points are concentrated. The ITU’s advisory body lists geographic concentration and heavy reliance on a small number of cable systems among the main weaknesses, with small island states and least developed countries the most exposed [14].

A cable is a fixed asset on the seabed. Human activity and natural hazards break cables, repairs take time, and permits slow both building and mending [14]. Fibre also cannot reach a ship, an aircraft or a remote site, which is where radio and satellites come in.
4. Radio and laser links in space

A satellite network uses two kinds of link. Starlink’s published design gives each satellite Ku-band phased-array antennas and dual-band antennas to reach customers by radio, and three lasers to reach other satellites, each rated at up to 200 Gbps. The satellites orbit at about 550 km, which Starlink says brings latency to around 25 ms against more than 600 ms for a geostationary satellite [8]. So the dish on a roof talks to the satellite by radio, and the satellites talk to each other by laser. NASA has tested laser links far beyond Earth orbit: its Deep Space Optical Communications experiment sent ultra-high-definition video from 19 million miles away at 267 Mbps in December 2023, returned data from 288 million miles in July 2024, and made its 65th and final pass in September 2025 [10]. Laser data does not travel faster than radio data. The gain is a higher data rate from a narrower beam and a smaller, lighter terminal [11].
Phased-array beam steering: aim a radio beam electronically, with no moving dish, and follow a satellite across the sky.
Pointing, acquisition and tracking: find the other terminal and hold a narrow laser beam on it while both ends move.
Dynamic routing: recompute paths as satellites move and links appear and disappear.
Starlink publishes the most detail and sells a smaller laser terminal to other satellite makers, rated at 25 Gbps [8]. NASA’s demonstrations are public and documented mission by mission [10, 11].

A laser beam is narrow, and an error of a fraction of a degree can miss the target entirely. Clouds and mist interrupt optical links to the ground, so operators need several ground stations in different places [11]. The 200 Gbps figure is a published maximum for one link, not the capacity of the network or the speed a customer receives [8].
5. Orbital compute: data centres in space

The newest idea is to put the computer in orbit as well. Google announced Project Suncatcher on 4 November 2025 as research into a network of solar-powered satellites carrying its TPU AI chips [15]. In September 2026 it set out the reasoning and the problems. A satellite in the right low orbit is in near-constant sunlight and could collect up to eight times the solar power of a panel on the ground. In a vacuum, heat can leave only through radiators. The chips were tested in a proton beam for radiation tolerance, and laser links between satellites in a cluster are due to be tested in 2027 [16]. On 1 October 2026 a prototype built with Planet was launched on a SpaceX rideshare, contact was confirmed, and the mission will measure how the chips respond to radiation and temperature [17]. That is one satellite testing hardware. It is not a data centre.
Onboard inference: run the model next to the sensor and send down the result, not the raw data.
Fault-tolerant scheduling: assume nodes will fail and cannot be repaired, and move the work around them.
Formation control: every satellite must know its own position and where it sits relative to its neighbours [16].
Google, working with Planet, runs the programme with the most public documentation [15, 17]. Other organisations have announced plans; this report cites only what a primary source documents.

Nothing here has been shown at scale. Heat rejection, radiation damage, the impossibility of repair, launch and replacement cost, and the capacity to send results down are all open [16]. Every figure comes from the company doing the work, and there are no independent cost data yet.
6. The thought experiment: Sydney to California with no fibre

Suppose every land and submarine fibre vanished and a message still had to cross the Pacific. This is a thought experiment, not a forecast: cables carry over 99% of international data flows today [13]. It is useful because each hop uses a technology described above. What does not exist is the capacity to do it for everyone.
Create. A phone or laptop turns the message into packets, exactly as it does today.
Uplink. A user terminal sends the packets by radio to a satellite in view [8].
Relay. The satellite passes them from one satellite to the next over laser links [8].
Compute, if needed. A request that needs a model is routed to a satellite carrying processors. Today this exists only as a prototype [17].
Downlink. A satellite above the destination sends the packets down by radio, or by laser where the sky is clear [11].
Deliver. A local link carries them to the recipient, and the reply returns the same way.
“Satellites will make fibre obsolete.”
Submarine cables carry over 99% of international data flows [13], and the ITU’s 2026 work is about making them more resilient [14].
Not supported by the evidence
“Starlink beams lasers down to your dish.”
Customers are reached by phased-array radio antennas; the lasers link satellites to each other [8].
Wrong link: radio down, laser across
“Each Starlink laser link runs at 200 Gbps.”
Starlink publishes “up to 200 Gbps” for each inter-satellite laser [8].
Company-reported maximum
“Laser data travels faster than radio data.”
NASA states that the data does not travel faster; the gain is in how much can be sent [11].
False: same speed, higher data rate
“NASA has streamed video from deep space by laser.”
Ultra-high-definition video from 19 million miles away at 267 Mbps, December 2023 [10].
Demonstrated
“Deep-space laser links are now in routine use.”
The experiment made its 65th and final pass in September 2025 and is listed as completed [10].
A completed demonstration, not a service
“Laser links work in any weather.”
Clouds and mist interrupt optical links to the ground; several ground stations are the usual answer [11].
False for links to the ground
“There are already AI data centres in orbit.”
One prototype satellite was launched on 1 October 2026 to test chips [17]; two more are planned for 2027 [16].
Company-reported prototype
“Space gives eight times the solar power.”
Google writes “up to eight times”, for a satellite in the right low orbit [16].
Company-reported best case
“Cooling is free in space because space is cold.”
In a vacuum, heat can leave only through radiators, which calls for a different approach to cooling electronics [16].
False
“Radio, light and X-rays are different kinds of thing.”
All are electromagnetic radiation, set apart by wavelength, frequency and energy [3, 4].
Established physics: one spectrum
“Light is either a wave or a particle.”
It acts as a wave in some circumstances and as a beam of photons in others [2].
Established physics: both descriptions hold
“Microwaved food becomes radioactive.”
Microwaves make water molecules vibrate, which produces heat; the food does not become radioactive [9].
False
“Charles Kao invented fibre optics.”
Glass fibres existed from the 1930s. Kao showed that very pure glass would carry light far enough [1]; the laser came from Maiman in 1960 [12].
Partly: one of several breakthroughs
“A fibre-free internet is possible.”
Each hop exists or has been demonstrated [8, 10]. The capacity to replace cables carrying over 99% of traffic does not [13].
Thought experiment
Will satellites replace fibre-optic cables?

Not on current evidence. Submarine cables carry over 99% of international data flows, and the ITU is working on making them more resilient. Satellites add coverage for remote places, ships and aircraft, and a second path when a cable fails. The likely future is a layered network that uses fibre, radio and satellite links together.
Does Starlink use lasers?

Yes, between satellites. Starlink says each satellite carries three lasers rated at up to 200 Gbps that link it to other satellites. The connection from a satellite to a customer’s dish is radio, using phased-array antennas, not a laser.
What is the difference between an optical amplifier and a regenerator?

An optical amplifier makes the light stronger without reading the data, and it amplifies noise along with the signal. A regenerator detects the data, decides what each symbol was, and sends a fresh, clean signal. Long fibre routes rely mainly on amplifiers, with error-correcting codes repairing the errors that remain.
Why do networks use lasers and not sunlight?

Both are light, but a laser is narrow in colour, tightly directed and easy to switch in a controlled way, so a transmitter can impose a known pattern on it and aim it at a receiver. Sunlight is broad, spread out and carries no pattern from the sender. It mostly shows up as background noise at the detector.
Why does a microwave oven heat food?

A device called a magnetron produces microwaves, which are electromagnetic radiation like radio waves. They make water molecules in the food vibrate, and that vibration is heat. The US Food and Drug Administration states that this does not make food radioactive. It is the same kind of radiation used for communication, put to work delivering energy.
What is Project Suncatcher?

It is a Google research project, announced in November 2025, on running AI chips on solar-powered satellites linked by lasers. A prototype satellite built with Planet was launched on 1 October 2026 to measure how the chips handle radiation and temperature. Google describes it as research, with two more satellites planned for 2027.
Is satellite internet slower than fibre?

It depends on the orbit. A geostationary satellite sits about 35,786 km up, and Starlink puts the resulting delay above 600 ms. Low-orbit satellites at about 550 km bring that to around 25 ms by Starlink’s figures. Fibre still offers far more total capacity between cities and data centres.
What should a business do with this now?

Treat the link as a design constraint. Decide where each model runs (on the device, at a gateway or in a data centre) from the bandwidth and delay it can count on, monitor the links you depend on, and plan a second path for the ones that matter. Orbital computing is worth watching, not planning around.

blog.posts.22.snippet: Data centres in orbit make headlines. The useful question is closer to home: what does the link under your model allow, and where should the model sit?
blogDetail.posts.where-ai-runs-fibre-sat: Will AI Run in Orbit? What the Link Decides About Where You Run Yours
Where AI Runs: Device, Cloud or Orbit
A model is only as responsive as the link under it. How bandwidth, delay and outages decide where AI should run, from the device to orbit.
13 October 2026
The link comes first

On 1 October 2026 a prototype satellite went into orbit to test how AI chips cope with radiation and temperature. It is a real experiment, and it is one satellite. Our evidence report on signals, fibre and satellites sets out what it does and does not show.

The lesson for anyone building with AI today is less exotic. Every model sits on top of a link, and the link decides how fast an answer can come back, how much data can reach the model, and what happens when the connection drops. Decide that first, and the question of where the model should run mostly answers itself.
1. Know what the link gives you
Three numbers describe a link well enough to design against. Measure them where the system will actually run, not in the office.
Delay. Starlink puts a low-orbit satellite link at around 25 ms and a geostationary one above 600 ms. A voice assistant can live with the first and not with the second.
Capacity. A camera produces far more data than most remote links can carry. If the raw data cannot travel, the model has to go to the data.
Availability. Cables break and clouds interrupt laser links to the ground. Ask how often the link is down and for how long, and get the answer from logs.
2. Put the model where the data is
There are three places a model can run, and most systems end up using more than one.
On the device or at the edge, when the delay budget is tight or the raw data is too large to send. Models are smaller here, so measure what accuracy you give up.
At a gateway or regional site, when several devices share one model and the link to them is good.
In a data centre, when the work is heavy and can wait. This is still where almost everything runs, on the far side of fibre that carries over 99% of international data flows.
3. Design for the link failing
A system that only works with a perfect connection will fail in the field. The behaviour during an outage has to be designed, and then tested by pulling the plug.
Queue and resume. Work that cannot be sent waits in a durable queue and goes when the link returns, in order and without duplicates.
Degrade on purpose. A smaller local model answers when the large one is out of reach, and says that it is the fallback.
Monitor the link like a model. Track delay, loss and outage time next to accuracy and drift, and alert on a trend before it becomes a failure.
4. What orbit changes, and what it does not
Computing in orbit is the same decision taken one step further: run the model next to data that is already in space, and send down only the result. Where that fits, it is a sensible idea.
It suits data that starts in orbit, such as Earth observation, where sending every raw image down is the bottleneck.
It does not remove the hard parts. Heat leaves only through radiators, hardware cannot be repaired, and results still need a link to the ground.
It is not a reason to change plans now. What exists is a prototype reported by the company that built it, with more tests planned for 2027.
Where to start

Pick one model that matters and write down the delay it can tolerate, the data it needs and what should happen when its link is down. Measure the real link against those three lines. The gap between them is the work.
The full analysis, with the source for every figure and six step-through diagrams from the voice to the satellite, is in the evidence report.

Link Health Monitoring for Networks

How we would build link health monitoring for a satellite or network operator: one telemetry pipeline, anomaly detection and alerts with context.

A network or satellite operator runs thousands of links, and each one reports signal level, error rate, delay and weather exposure to a different system. Degradation shows up as a slow trend long before it becomes an outage, but nobody sees the trend because nobody sees the metrics together. The operations desk hears about a failing link when customers do.

The approach: bring link telemetry into one pipeline, learn what normal looks like for each link, and raise an alert when a link leaves that range, with the evidence attached. The models are simple on purpose. The value is in clean data, stated thresholds and an alert that an operator can act on without opening four other tools.
Discovery. We map the telemetry sources, the decisions the operations desk makes from them, and which failures cost the most.
One pipeline. Telemetry is validated on arrival, time-aligned and stored with its lineage, so every alert can be traced back to the readings behind it.
Detection. Per-link baselines flag anomalies and slow drift in error rate, delay and signal level, with weather and maintenance windows as context.
Proof before trust. The detector runs against recorded outages first, and its misses and false alarms are counted before any alert reaches the desk.
A single view of link health in place of separate tools.
Alerts that carry the readings and the trend that triggered them.
A measured false-alarm and miss rate from replayed outages, reported before go-live.
Monitoring of the detector itself, so drift in the models is caught like drift in a link.
A runbook for each alert type, with the step a person must approve.

4F² DRAM: the cell redesign explained
Evidence report: how a DRAM cell stores a bit, what moving from 6F² to 4F² changes, and what it means for AI systems. 39 sources.
Evidence report · Semiconductor analysis
Semiconductors
Global
DRAM cell architecture and memory for AI systems

Evidence report. Diagrams are schematics, not any maker's layout. Area and density figures are idealised geometry unless a source is cited. Company figures are company-reported and have not been independently verified. Sources were read on 13 October 2026; most IEEE papers were read as abstracts.

For many AI workloads the limiting resource is memory, not arithmetic. Peak server compute has grown about 3.0× every two years while DRAM bandwidth has grown about 1.6× [31], and a model that does not fit in memory does not run. That memory is DRAM, and since the early 2010s it has been built on one cell layout, known as 6F² [15, 7]. The layout is near its limit [8]. In October 2026 CXMT became the latest maker to describe a move to a smaller cell, 4F², in a conference talk reported by the trade press [37, 38]. Samsung, SK hynix, and Kioxia with Nanya have published their own versions in peer-reviewed venues [12, 14, 16]. Headlines turned the geometry into a promise of 50% more memory. The engineering says something more careful.

This report explains the cell from first principles, then tests the claims made about it. It covers how one transistor and one capacitor hold a bit [1], how the bit is read and rewritten [3], why a 4F² footprint needs a transistor that stands upright [10], what has to change in patterning, capacitors and wafer bonding to build one [22, 19, 14], and where DRAM sits among the memories of an AI server [28, 29]. Every statement is tied to a peer-reviewed paper, a standard, a patent or a named company statement, and is labelled for the kind of evidence it is.
Sources first. Peer-reviewed papers, JEDEC standards and patents carry the physics. Company statements are used only for what the company said, and are labelled company-reported.
Geometry is kept apart from product. A cell-area ratio is arithmetic. A capacity, a yield or a ship date is a claim that needs its own evidence.
Every diagram is a schematic. None reproduces a maker's layout, and the idealised models are marked as models.
Where Algorythmos fits: we do not design memory chips. We size, deploy and monitor AI systems, and memory capacity and bandwidth are inputs to that work.
A 4F² cell covers two thirds of the area of a 6F² cell: 33.3% less area, or 1.5 times the cells in the same array area. That is arithmetic, not a measurement.
The whole chip gains less. Sense amplifiers and wordline drivers alone take roughly 13% to 25% of a commodity DRAM die, and they do not shrink with the cell [9].
4F² needs a vertical-channel transistor. Working devices and arrays have been published by CXMT, Samsung, SK hynix, and Kioxia with Nanya [11, 12, 14, 16].
No maker has published yield or cost per bit for a 4F² product. CXMT's server module is a reported plan, with no specifications disclosed [37, 38].
4F² is not 3D DRAM. One shrinks the footprint of a single layer of cells; the other stacks layers, with 5 and 16 demonstrated so far [26, 27].
For AI, denser DRAM means more capacity per module or stack. It does not by itself raise bandwidth, which the interface sets [30].

One transistor, one capacitor: how DRAM stores a bit
Hold one bit as electric charge, and give it back on request.

A DRAM cell is a single transistor and a single capacitor, the arrangement Robert Dennard patented for IBM in 1968 [1]. The capacitor is charged through the transistor to store the bit [1]. To read it, the bitline is first set to half the supply voltage; then the wordline opens the transistor and the charge spreads onto the bitline [2, 3]. The bitline's capacitance is about ten times the cell's, so the bitline moves by only a few per cent of the supply voltage [4]. A sense amplifier detects that small shift and drives the bitline to a full level, which also refills the capacitor [3]. The read destroys the stored value, and the amplifier puts it back [1, 4].
Signal on the bitline: ΔV ≈ (Vdd ÷ 2) × Ccell ÷ (Ccell + Cbitline) [4].
With Ccell about one tenth of Cbitline, ΔV is about 4.5% of Vdd [4].
Capacitance to maintain: about 25 fF per cell [19].
Refresh: every cell rewritten within 64 ms [2].

Charge leaks away, so every cell has to be rewritten periodically. The interval has stayed at 64 ms across several DRAM generations [2]. A smaller cell must still hold enough charge to be sensed, and keeping capacitance near 25 fF per cell gets harder as cells shrink [19].
The array and the circuits around it
Find one cell among billions, read it, and leave every other cell intact.

Cells sit where wordlines cross bitlines. Selecting a wordline opens a whole row, and a sense amplifier on each bitline reads and restores every cell in that row [3]. Each sense amplifier is around a hundred times the size of a cell, so cells are grouped into blocks, typically 512 or 1,024 lines on a side, that share a strip of amplifiers [3]. Modern chips use the open-bitline arrangement [3], which is what made the 6F² cell possible [5]. Around the array sit wordline drivers, decoders, and the spare rows and columns that replace defective ones [9].

These circuits are overhead. In a typical commodity DRAM, bitline sense amplifiers take 8% to 15% of the die and local wordline drivers another 5% to 10% [9]. Designers call the cells' share of the die the array efficiency, and work to keep it high [9]. A denser cell also brings bitlines closer together, and modelling of 4F² arrays identifies coupling between neighbouring bitlines as a first-order problem [18].
From 6F² to 4F²: the geometry
Fit more cells into the same silicon without making F any smaller.

F is the smallest feature a layout uses, and cell area is quoted in multiples of F² [5]. Earlier cells took 8F² [17]; an open and folded bitline arrangement proposed in 1994 brought the cell to 6F² [5]. With its wordline buried below the silicon surface, the 6F² cell has carried DRAM from 46 nm to today's 10 nm-class generations [6, 15]. A 4F² cell is 2F by 2F [39], which the industry roadmap calls the practical limit for a cell with one transistor and one capacitor [8]. Going from 6 to 4 removes a third of the area, so 1.5 times as many cells fit in the same array. An early Samsung 4F² design estimated about 30% more gross dies per wafer than 6F² [17].
Cell area: 4F² ÷ 6F² = 2/3, a reduction of 33.3%.
Cells per array area: 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5×.
Whole die, if a share p of it is cell array and nothing else changes: new area = 1 − p/3 of the old.
Example: at p = 60% the die shrinks by 20%, or holds 25% more bits at the same size. Illustrative, not a measured product.

The 1.5× applies to the array alone. Everything outside it stays, so the gain for a whole chip depends on how much of the die is array [9]. Reporting on CXMT's announcement put the expected density gain at 30% to 50%, and noted that early products may adopt 4F² only in part [37].
The vertical-channel transistor
Switch the capacitor on and off from inside a column two F wide.

In today's 6F² cell the transistor is a saddle-fin device with its wordline buried below the surface [7, 6]. Its source and drain still sit side by side, and that costs area. A 4F² cell stands the channel upright as a pillar, with the bitline buried beneath it and the capacitor on top [10]. The gate can then surround the channel. CXMT's 2023 paper reported a gate-all-around, junctionless vertical transistor with an on/off current ratio above 10⁹ and a sub-threshold swing of 62.5 mV per decade [10], and a companion paper an 8 Gb array at 198 Mbit/mm² [11]. Lower bitline capacitance is a stated benefit of the vertical cell [10].

Samsung has published a silicon cell with a back gate shared between neighbouring cells [12], and an oxide-channel vertical transistor that can be built on top of the peripheral circuits [13]. SK hynix has shown a vertical-gate 4F² array integrated over its periphery [14]. Kioxia and Nanya demonstrated a 275 Mbit array with an oxide-channel transistor built on top of the capacitor [16]. CXMT described a vertical surrounded-gate transistor as the basis of its 4F² platform in October 2026 [37, 38].

The buried bitline is harder to form than in a conventional cell [10]. Thin, tall silicon structures bend and lean during processing [12]. Tightly packed bitlines couple to one another [18]. These are the problems the published papers set out to solve; none of them reports a product yield.
Printing the pattern
Make lines and pillars finer than lithography can print in one exposure.

Spacer-based pitch multiplication deposits a thin film on the sides of printed lines, removes the lines and keeps the film: two lines where there was one, at half the pitch [22]. Doing it twice gives a quarter of the printed pitch [22]. CXMT formed the pillars of its vertical transistor by applying double patterning twice, at right angles [10], and states that its fifth-generation platform reaches an 11.95 nm half-pitch with quadruple patterning [36]. Samsung built its 20 nm DRAM without extreme-ultraviolet lithography [20], and at 14 nm used five extreme-ultraviolet layers, cutting process steps by about 20% [21].

Lines made this way are never printed directly. Their spacing depends on the width of each printed line and each film, and uneven spacing is a known result [22]. Each extra patterning pass also adds process steps, which is what extreme-ultraviolet lithography reduces [21].
The capacitor, and building the logic separately
Keep enough charge in a shrinking footprint, and stop the periphery eating the gain.

A capacitor's footprint shrinks with the cell, so it grows upward instead. Modern cells use tall, high-aspect-ratio capacitors with a zirconia, alumina, zirconia dielectric between titanium nitride electrodes [19]. The roadmap expects the shape to change from a cylinder to a pillar [8]. Samsung's 20 nm generation gained 21% capacitance at the same cell size from a honeycomb arrangement [20]. CXMT states a capacitor aspect ratio of 45:1 for its fifth-generation platform [36]. The second lever is to stop spending die area on logic: build the cell array on one wafer and the peripheral circuits on another, then bond them, as is already done in 3D NAND flash [23]. SK hynix has demonstrated a 4F² array bonded over its periphery [14], and Samsung has shown the same idea for the existing 6F² cell [24].

Tall, narrow structures are sensitive to their etched profile, which changes both leakage and capacitance [19]. Bonding adds alignment and contact steps between wafers [14]. Samsung has also published an alternative that builds oxide transistors over the periphery with no bonding at all [13]. Which route a given product takes is for its maker to state; reporting on CXMT's announcement noted that no specifications were disclosed [38].
Where DRAM sits in an AI system
Hold models and their working data close enough, and fast enough, for the processors that use them.

An AI server uses several memories. SRAM inside the chips is the fastest but takes six transistors per bit, so it holds far fewer bits per area than DRAM [34]. NAND flash keeps data without power and stores it as trapped electrons, a different cell altogether [34, 35]. DRAM is the working memory, in two forms. DDR5 devices of 8 Gb to 32 Gb are assembled into modules for the processor [28]. High-bandwidth memory stacks DRAM dies and couples them tightly to the accelerator [29]; the HBM4 standard allows stacks 4 to 16 dies high, with a 2,048-bit interface and up to 2 TB/s [30]. For serving large models the bottleneck is increasingly memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic [31], and the memory each request needs limits how many requests can be batched together [32].
More bits per die, so more capacity in a module or stack of the same size.
No direct change to bandwidth, which the interface and its number of connections set [30].
Capacity can also be added outside the module, through CXL memory expansion [33].
HBM is built from DRAM dies [29], so a cell change could reach accelerators too. No 4F² HBM is reported in the sources used here.
Compute has been growing faster than memory: about 3.0× every two years for peak server compute, against 1.6× for DRAM bandwidth [31]. A denser cell adds capacity. It does not close that gap.
4F² is not 3D DRAM
Keep two different ideas apart.

In a 4F² cell the transistor is vertical, but the array is still a single layer of cells. 3D DRAM is a different step: the capacitors are laid horizontally and whole layers of cells are stacked [27], so density rises with the number of layers rather than with a smaller footprint [25]. SK hynix has demonstrated a full chip with five stacked layers [26], and Samsung a 16-layer structure [27]. The roadmap sees no clear path for further scaling beyond the planar cell [8], which is why both routes are being pursued.

Samsung calls its version vertically stacked DRAM [25, 27]. SK hynix builds its layers from sacrificial silicon and silicon-germanium films and joins the stack to its logic by hybrid wafer bonding [26].
The papers cited here report demonstrations, not products [26, 27].
From an announced architecture to memory you can buy

An architecture is the first of several steps. A server module must also meet the DDR5 device standard [28], be validated by the makers of the platforms it goes into, ship in volume, and cost no more per good bit than what it replaces. Each step needs its own evidence. On the evidence in this report, 4F² has peer-reviewed prototypes from several makers and one reported plan for a server module.

What does 4F² mean?

F is the smallest feature a chip's layout uses. A 4F² cell occupies a square two F on each side; today's standard cell occupies 6F². It is a measure of layout area per bit, not the name of a manufacturing node.
Does 4F² mean 50% more memory?

Only for the cell array, and only on paper. A square of silicon holds 1.5 times as many 4F² cells as 6F² cells. The circuits around the array do not shrink, so a whole chip gains less, and no maker has published a measured figure for a product.
Is 4F² the same as 3D DRAM?

No. In a 4F² cell the transistor stands upright, but the memory is still one layer of cells. 3D DRAM stacks several layers of cells on top of one another. Both raise density; they are separate technologies at different stages.
Why does DRAM need refreshing?

Each bit is a small charge on a capacitor, and the charge leaks away. The chip therefore reads and rewrites every cell on a fixed schedule, typically within 64 milliseconds. That is the D in DRAM: dynamic.
Will 4F² make AI models run faster?

Not by itself. A denser cell puts more bits on a chip, which raises the capacity of a module or a memory stack. Speed in serving large models is limited mostly by memory bandwidth, which depends on the interface, not on the cell.
Who is working on 4F² DRAM?

Peer-reviewed demonstrations have come from CXMT, Samsung, SK hynix, and Kioxia with Nanya. In October 2026 CXMT was reported to be planning a server memory module by the end of the year, with no specifications disclosed.
Does Algorythmos design memory chips?
No. Algorythmos builds and operates AI systems: models, pipelines and monitoring. Memory capacity and bandwidth are constraints we plan around, which is why we follow the hardware closely.

blog.posts.23.snippet: A smaller memory cell made headlines as 50% more memory. The useful question is closer to home: how much memory do your models need, and of which kind?
blogDetail.posts.why-memory-density-matt: Does 4F² DRAM Change Your AI Plans? How to Size Memory for the Models You Run
Sizing Memory for AI: What 4F² Changes
Memory, not arithmetic, limits many AI workloads. What a denser DRAM cell changes, what it does not, and how to size capacity and bandwidth today.
13 October 2026
Memory comes first

In October 2026 a DRAM maker described a move to a smaller memory cell, known as 4F², and headlines turned it into 50% more memory. Our evidence report on the 4F² DRAM cell sets out what the geometry gives and what has not been shown: the cell is a third smaller, the whole chip gains less, and no maker has published yield or cost for a product.

The lesson for anyone running AI today is more practical. For serving large models the bottleneck is increasingly memory rather than arithmetic, and a model that does not fit in memory does not run at all. Size the memory first, then choose the hardware.
1. Know which memory you are short of
An AI server has several memories, and they are not interchangeable. Find out which one limits you before buying more of anything.
Accelerator memory. High-bandwidth memory sits beside the accelerator and holds the model while it runs. If the weights and the working data do not fit here, nothing else matters.
System memory. DDR5 modules beside the processor hold everything on its way in and out: data being prepared, models being loaded, the services around the model.
Storage. Flash keeps models and data with the power off. It sets how long a cold start takes.
2. Separate capacity from bandwidth
Capacity is how much fits. Bandwidth is how fast it moves. They run out in different ways, and a denser cell helps only the first.
Capacity runs out as models, context and batch size grow. The memory each request needs limits how many requests can be served together.
Bandwidth runs out when processors can compute faster than memory can feed them. Peak server compute has grown about 3.0× every two years, against about 1.6× for DRAM bandwidth.
The interface sets bandwidth. The HBM4 standard allows up to 2 TB/s across a 2,048-bit interface, and a change to the cell does not alter that.
3. Measure before you size
A sizing taken from a model card is a guess. Measure on the workload you will actually run.
Peak memory per request, at the context lengths your users really send, not the average.
Requests served together at your target response time. Raise the batch until memory or response time gives way, and note which gave way first.
Headroom. Leave room for the next model version and for a traffic peak. A system sized to fit exactly fails on its first busy day.
4. What a denser cell changes, and what it does not
A 4F² cell is a step the industry has taken many times before: more bits in the same silicon. Where it arrives, it is good news for capacity.
It raises capacity per module or stack, once products built on it are qualified and shipping. The published work so far is prototypes.
It does not raise bandwidth, and it is not 3D DRAM, which stacks layers of cells and is a separate technology.
It is not a reason to change plans now. A server module was reported as planned for the end of 2026, with no specifications disclosed.
Where to start

Pick the model that matters most and write down three numbers: the memory it needs per request, how many requests it must serve at once, and the response time you have promised. Measure the system you have against them. The gap between them is the work.
The full analysis, with the source for every figure, nine step-through diagrams and a calculator for the whole-chip gain, is in the evidence report.
